title: Artificial immunity and vaccines
covers: Active versus passive immunity, herd immunity, the types of vaccine with their strengths and limits, adjuvants, and vaccination against cancer.

items.p: Passive immunity is borrowed antibody. It works at once but is temporary and leaves no memory.
Active immunity is the person's own response. It takes time but usually lasts, with memory.

table: Maternal antibody; IgA in breast milk and colostrum

items.p: A non-pathogenic biological product that imitates the pathogen's antigens. It induces protection without causing the disease, and it must pass clinical trials like any drug.
An ideal vaccine is safe, effective, long-lasting, easy to give, heat-stable, cheap and easy to mass-produce. Latency and antigenic variation of the pathogen make vaccines harder to design.
When enough people are immune, transmission stops and the unprotected are protected indirectly.

ul: Highly transmissible disease (measles): about 95% coverage needed
Less transmissible (polio, rubella, diphtheria): about 85% may be enough

table: Whole organism destroyed by chemicals, heat or radiation
Stable; weak response; boosters. Hepatitis A, rabies, injectable polio and influenza
Strong, lasting immunity in 1–2 doses; needs refrigeration; can revert; avoid in the immunocompromised. Measles, mumps, chickenpox, yellow fever, BCG
Few side effects; weak, needs adjuvant. Hepatitis B
T-independent: no memory, low affinity, no response under 2 years. Pneumococcus 23
Polysaccharide linked to a protein carrier
T-dependent: memory, works in infants. Hib
Immunity to the toxin, not the microbe. Diphtheria, tetanus
Harmless virus carrying the antigen gene
Strong response without adjuvant; pre-existing immunity to the vector is a problem
DNA or mRNA encoding the antigen
Fast to design. Pfizer and Moderna mRNA vaccines

items.p: DNA vaccines are stable at room temperature but must reach the nucleus. RNA vaccines act in the cytoplasm but are less stable.

items.note: The slide says inactivated vaccines "do not require refrigeration"; in practice most still need a cold chain. The slide also lists cholera among toxoid vaccines; standard sources describe cholera vaccines as killed or live oral vaccines.

summary.h: Live versus non-live in weak immune systems

ul: Live vaccines can replicate without control in immunocompromised patients
Non-live vaccines are safe for them, but may not protect if B cells are missing (B-cell or combined immunodeficiency)

items.p: Adjuvants make a vaccine more immunogenic. They behave like PAMPs: they wake up innate immunity and antigen-presenting cells.

ul: Delivery systems: concentrate and display the antigen
Immune potentiators: activate innate immunity directly

items.p: Other ingredients are preservatives, emulsifiers (polysorbate 80) and stabilizers (gelatine, sorbitol). The main concern is allergy.

ul: Prevent infections that cause cancer: HPV 16 and 18 (cervix), hepatitis B (liver)
Make "cold" tumors visible to the immune system ("hot"), so checkpoint blockade can work

items.note: The slide groups Helicobacter pylori (stomach cancer) with cancer-causing viruses. It is a bacterium, and no vaccine against it is licensed.

cards.q: Passive immunity: definition and two limits
cards.a: Transfer of preformed antibodies; temporary and no memory.
Maternal antibody; IgA in breast milk and colostrum
Pooled immune globulin (IVIG), antivenin
Indirect protection of susceptible people because transmission is interrupted

cards.q: Vaccine coverage needed for measles versus polio or rubella
cards.a: About 95% versus about 85%

cards.q: Two pathogen features that make vaccines difficult
cards.a: Latency and antigenic variation
Weak immune response; booster doses needed
Hepatitis A, rabies, injectable polio, injectable influenza, typhoid
Strong cellular and antibody responses; long-term immunity after 1–2 doses
Need refrigeration, can revert to virulence, dangerous in immunocompromised patients
Measles, mumps, chickenpox, yellow fever, BCG, oral polio, nasal influenza

cards.q: Why does a plain polysaccharide vaccine work poorly in infants?
cards.a: The response is T-independent: no memory, no affinity maturation, no response under 2 years.

cards.q: What does conjugating a polysaccharide to a protein carrier achieve?
cards.a: A T-dependent response: memory, affinity maturation, protection in infants (example: Hib)

cards.q: Toxoid vaccines: how made, and what immunity
cards.a: Toxin inactivated with formalin; immunity to the toxin's effects (diphtheria, tetanus)

cards.q: Subunit vaccine example and its weakness
cards.a: Hepatitis B; poor immunogenicity, so adjuvants are needed

cards.q: Viral vector vaccines: advantage and drawback
cards.a: Strong humoral and cellular response without adjuvant; pre-existing immunity to the vector (solved with simian adenovirus)
DNA: stable at room temperature, must enter the nucleus. RNA: no nucleus needed, less stable.
Enhance immunogenicity by acting like PAMPs: activate innate immunity and APCs
Aluminum salts (alum)
HPV 16/18 (cervical cancer) and hepatitis B (liver cancer)

cards.q: Are non-live vaccines safe in immunodeficiency?
cards.a: Yes, but they may not protect when B cells are lacking.

questions.stem: A hiker bitten by a viper receives antivenin. Which type of immunization is this, and what is its main limitation?

options.A: Artificial active; temporary protection with no memory
options.B: Natural passive; long-term protection with memory
options.C: Artificial passive; temporary protection with no memory
options.D: Artificial passive; long-term protection once boosters are given
options.E: Natural active; protection delayed by one to two weeks

questions.explanation: Passive immunization transfers preformed antibodies to an unimmunized individual: temporary immunity, no memory. Antivenin and pooled human immune gamma globulin are artificial passive immunization. A: Antivenin is preformed antibody, so it is passive. B: It is artificial, and passive immunity leaves no memory. D: Passive immunity ends when the antibodies are destroyed. E: No immune response of the recipient is induced.

questions.stem: How does active immunization differ from passive immunization?

options.A: The person receives preformed antibodies, typically giving long-term immunity
options.B: The person's own immune system is stimulated, but immunity is lost once the antibodies are destroyed
options.C: The person receives primed T cells from an immunized donor
options.D: The person's innate system is stimulated without any adaptive response
options.E: The person's own immune system is stimulated, typically giving long-term immunity

questions.explanation: Active immunization occurs with exposure of an unimmunized individual to a pathogenic agent; the immune system develops immunity, typically long-term. A: Preformed antibodies define passive immunization. B: That is the limitation of passive immunity. C: Not the definition given. D: Active immunization develops adaptive immunity.

questions.stem: Which example is matched with the correct type of immunity?

options.A: IgA in breast milk and colostrum: natural active
options.B: IgA in breast milk and colostrum: natural passive
options.C: IVIG in an immunocompromised patient: artificial active
options.D: Infection with a pathogen: natural passive
options.E: Vaccination: artificial passive

questions.explanation: Natural passive: maternal Ig, IgA in breast milk and colostrum. Artificial passive: pooled human immune gamma globulin, antivenin, IVIG. Natural active: infection. Artificial active: vaccination. A: The infant receives preformed antibody. C: IVIG is preformed antibody: artificial passive. D: Infection induces the person's own response: natural active. E: Vaccination is artificial active.

questions.stem: Which term describes vaccination, and what distinguishes it from natural infection?

options.A: Artificial passive immunity; it supplies antibody without stimulating the immune system
options.B: Natural active immunity; it produces a mild form of the disease
options.C: Artificial active immunity; it gives temporary protection without memory
options.D: Artificial active immunity; stimulation without active disease
options.E: Natural passive immunity; it transfers maternal antibody

questions.explanation: Artificial active immunizations mimic the stimulation necessary for immune development yet do not produce active disease. A: Vaccination stimulates the recipient's immune system. B: It is artificial and designed not to cause active disease. C: Active immunity is typically long-term. E: Not vaccination.

questions.stem: Which statement about vaccines matches the lecture's definition?

options.A: A non-pathogenic biological product that, like other drugs, requires clinical trials
options.B: A pathogenic biological product that causes mild disease and, unlike other drugs, is exempt from clinical trials
options.C: A preparation of preformed antibodies that neutralizes the pathogen on later exposure
options.D: A non-pathogenic chemical that blocks pathogen replication during infection
options.E: A biological product that confers protection without inducing an immune response

questions.explanation: A vaccine is a biological product that safely induces an immune response conferring protection on subsequent exposure; it is non-pathogenic, mimics pathogenic antigens, and requires validation through clinical trials. B: It is non-pathogenic and needs clinical trials. C: That is passive immunization. D: That describes an antimicrobial drug. E: Protection comes from the induced immune response.

questions.stem: What is herd immunity, as defined in the take-home messages?

options.A: Each vaccinated person is directly protected by a high antibody titer
options.B: Maternal antibodies protect infants of vaccinated mothers
options.C: The pathogen mutates until it no longer causes disease
options.D: Unvaccinated people acquire memory cells from vaccinated contacts
options.E: Indirect protection of the susceptible as transmission stops

questions.explanation: Herd immunity (herd protection) is reached when transmission of a pathogen is interrupted and incidence falls as a result of the indirect protection of individuals who would otherwise be susceptible. A: That is direct protection. B: That is natural passive immunity. C: Not herd immunity. D: Protection is indirect, by interrupted transmission.

questions.stem: What vaccine coverage does the lecture give for preventing outbreaks of a highly transmissible pathogen such as measles, compared with less transmissible ones such as polio, rubella or diphtheria?

options.A: About 85% for measles; about 95% for the others
options.B: About 95% for measles; about 85% for the others
options.C: About 75% for measles; about 50% for the others
options.D: About 95% for both groups
options.E: About 99% for measles; about 95% for the others

questions.explanation: For highly transmissible pathogens (measles) around 95% of the population must be vaccinated; for less transmissible organisms (polio, rubella, diphtheria) about 85% may be sufficient. A: Reversed. C: Not the figures given. D: A lower coverage may suffice for less transmissible organisms. E: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a requirement of an ideal vaccine EXCEPT:

options.A: Safety, without interfering with the host's immune response
options.B: Easy administration and thermal stability
options.C: Manufacture on a large scale at low cost
options.D: Replication in the host to maintain antigen exposure
options.E: Efficacy with a persistent immune response

questions.explanation: Requirements: safety, efficacy, nature and persistence of the immune response, easy administration and thermal stability, large-scale manufacture, low cost. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which two pathogen properties are named as challenges to vaccine efficacy and long-term immunity?

options.A: The ability to induce latency and a polysaccharide capsule
options.B: Antigenic variation and a large genome
options.C: The ability to induce latency and antigenic variation
options.D: Extracellular replication and toxin production
options.E: High transmissibility and thermal instability

questions.explanation: The ability of pathogens to induce latency or to mutate (antigenic variation) negatively affects vaccine efficacy and long-term immunity. A: The second factor named is antigenic variation (mutation). B: Latency is the other factor. D: Not the factors named. E: Not the factors named.

questions.stem: For the same pathogen there may be several vaccine types. In the generation scheme of vaccine types, which assignment is correct?

options.A: First: live attenuated and inactivated; second: subunit, toxoid, conjugate; third generation: DNA and vector
options.B: First generation: subunit and toxoid; second: live attenuated and inactivated; third generation: conjugate
options.C: First generation: live attenuated and toxoid; second: inactivated and conjugate; third generation: subunit
options.D: First generation: DNA and recombinant vector; second: subunit; third generation: live attenuated
options.E: First generation: live attenuated and inactivated; second: DNA and viral vector; third generation: toxoid and conjugate

questions.explanation: First generation: live attenuated, inactivated. Second generation: subunit, toxoid, conjugate. Third generation: DNA, recombinant vector. For the same pathogen there may be several vaccine types. B: The first two generations are swapped. C: Toxoid and subunit are second generation. D: Reversed. E: Second and third are swapped.

questions.stem: Which statement about inactivated (killed) vaccines matches the lecture?

options.A: The organism is weakened by culture; responses are strong, so one or two doses suffice
options.B: A purified toxin is treated with formalin; immunity is to the toxin
options.C: The entire organism is destroyed by chemicals; responses are strong and lifelong after one dose
options.D: Pieces of the organism are purified; an adjuvant is rarely needed
options.E: The whole organism is destroyed; responses are weak, so booster shots are needed

questions.explanation: Inactivated vaccines are produced by destroying the entire pathogenic agent with chemicals, heat or radiation; they are harmless and stable (the slide says no refrigeration is needed and they can be freeze-dried), but induce weak responses and need boosters. A: That describes live attenuated vaccines. B: That describes toxoid vaccines. C: Responses are weak and boosters are required. D: That resembles subunit vaccines, which do need adjuvants.

questions.stem: Which list contains inactivated vaccines given as examples in the lecture?

options.A: Hepatitis A, measles and oral polio
options.B: Hepatitis B, rabies and yellow fever
options.C: Hepatitis A, rabies and injectable polio
options.D: Rabies, mumps and nasal influenza
options.E: BCG, chickenpox and injectable influenza

questions.explanation: Examples: typhoid, hepatitis A, rabies, injectable polio (versus the oral live form), injectable influenza (versus the live nasal spray). A: Measles and oral polio are live vaccines. B: Hepatitis B is a subunit vaccine and yellow fever is live. D: Mumps and the nasal influenza spray are live. E: BCG and chickenpox are live attenuated.

questions.stem: Why are live attenuated vaccines easier to produce for viruses than for bacteria?

options.A: Viruses grow faster in culture, so weakening takes less time
options.B: Bacteria cannot be cultured outside a host
options.C: Viral antigens are more immunogenic than bacterial antigens
options.D: Viruses have fewer genes
options.E: Bacteria revert to virulence less often than viruses

questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines are easily produced when the pathogen is a virus and hard when it is a bacterium, because viruses have fewer genes, making viral characteristics easier to control. A: The reason given is the smaller number of genes. B: Not the reason given. C: Not the reason given. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: A patient on chemotherapy asks about a yellow fever vaccine before travel. Which properties of this vaccine type are relevant?

options.A: Live attenuated: strong immunity after one to two doses; risky if immunocompromised
options.B: Inactivated: weak immunity needing boosters, and no risk in the immunocompromised
options.C: Live attenuated: weak immunity needing boosters, but safe in the immunocompromised
options.D: Toxoid: immunity to the toxin, and no risk in the immunocompromised
options.E: Subunit: few side effects, and no risk in the immunocompromised

questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines produce strong cellular and antibody responses and long-term immunity with one to two doses (e.g. yellow fever), but can be harmful if patients are immunocompromised (uncontrolled replication). B: Yellow fever vaccine is live attenuated. C: Live vaccines give strong immunity and can be harmful in the immunocompromised. D: Not a toxoid vaccine. E: Not a subunit vaccine.

questions.stem: Besides risk in immunocompromised patients, which two drawbacks of live attenuated vaccines does the lecture give?

options.A: Booster doses are required, and immunogenicity is weak
options.B: Refrigeration is needed, and reversion to virulence is possible
options.C: An adjuvant is required, and antigen choice is difficult
options.D: Pre-existing immunity to the vector, and high purity requirements
options.E: No response in infants, and no memory B cells

questions.explanation: Because they contain living microorganisms, refrigeration is required to preserve potency, and there is the possibility of reversion to the original virulent form. A: Those are drawbacks of inactivated vaccines. C: Those apply to subunit vaccines. D: Those apply to viral vector vaccines. E: Those apply to plain polysaccharide vaccines.

questions.stem: Which statement about BCG is correct?

options.A: A killed version of the bacterium causing tuberculosis in humans; used routinely in the US
options.B: A toxoid of the tuberculosis bacterium; used in many European countries
options.C: A weakened version of the measles virus; used worldwide
options.D: A weakened bovine tuberculosis bacterium; rarely used in the US
options.E: A subunit of the bovine tuberculosis bacterium given with alum

questions.explanation: BCG is a weakened version of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis in cows; it is used against tuberculosis in many European countries but rarely in the US. Other live examples: measles, mumps, chickenpox. A: It is live attenuated, bovine, and rarely used in the US. B: It is a live attenuated vaccine. C: BCG is bacterial. E: It is a whole weakened organism.

questions.stem: Which set of features describes subunit vaccines?

options.A: Fewer side effects, easy choice of antigens, strong immunogenicity without adjuvants; example hepatitis A
options.B: More side effects, risk of reversion, long-term immunity after one dose; example measles
options.C: Immunity to a toxin and not to the infection; example tetanus
options.D: Strong humoral and cellular responses without adjuvant; example Ebola
options.E: Fewer side effects, difficult choice of antigens, poor immunogenicity needing adjuvants; example hepatitis B

questions.explanation: Subunit vaccines include only pieces (epitopes, usually protein fragments): fewer side effects, but it is difficult to determine which antigens to include and immunogenicity may be poor, so adjuvants are used. Example: hepatitis B. They may be ineffective if the pathogen mutates. A: Antigen choice is difficult, adjuvants are needed, and the example is hepatitis B. B: That describes live attenuated vaccines. C: That describes toxoid vaccines. D: That describes viral vector vaccines.

questions.stem: How does a plain polysaccharide vaccine such as Pneumococcus 23 stimulate the immune system?

options.A: B cells respond in a T cell-dependent manner, giving memory and high-affinity antibody
options.B: T cells respond directly to the polysaccharide on MHC II
options.C: A T cell-independent B-cell response with low-affinity antibody
options.D: NK cells respond through Fc receptors, giving ADCC
options.E: B cells respond after the carrier protein is processed

questions.explanation: Polysaccharide vaccines are made from surface polysaccharides of invasive bacteria (meningococci, pneumococci) and stimulate B cells in a T-independent manner: poor immunogenicity and low-affinity antibody. A: That is the conjugate vaccine response. B: Polysaccharides are not presented to T cells this way. D: Not the mechanism. E: A plain polysaccharide vaccine has no carrier protein.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old receives a plain polysaccharide vaccine. According to the comparison figure, what is expected?

options.A: No immune response: the vaccine fails in infants under 2 years
options.B: A strong response with memory B cells, because polysaccharides cross-link receptors
options.C: A response limited to IgA in secretions
options.D: Affinity maturation but short-lived antibody
options.E: Reversion of the vaccine to a virulent form

questions.explanation: Polysaccharide vaccine: no memory B cells, short-lived antibody production, no affinity maturation, no immune response in infants under 2 years. The conjugate vaccine corrects these. B: Plain polysaccharide gives no memory, and infants under 2 do not respond. C: Not shown. D: There is no affinity maturation with plain polysaccharide. E: That concerns live vaccines.

questions.stem: How does a conjugate vaccine such as the Haemophilus b vaccine overcome the weakness of polysaccharide antigens?

options.A: The polysaccharide is mixed with aluminum salts, giving a T cell-independent response with memory
options.B: The polysaccharide is linked to a protein carrier, giving a T cell-dependent response
options.C: The polysaccharide is expressed by a viral vector, giving cellular immunity
options.D: The polysaccharide is replaced by an inactivated toxin
options.E: The polysaccharide is linked to a lipid carrier, giving stronger cross-linking of receptors

questions.explanation: A conjugate vaccine combines a weak antigen with a strong antigen as a carrier. Bacterial polysaccharide is chemically conjugated to a protein carrier (mostly tetanus toxoid, or diphtheria toxoid) giving a T-dependent response and immune memory. Example: Hib conjugate vaccine. A: The key is covalent linkage to a protein carrier and T-cell help. C: That is a viral vector vaccine. D: That is a toxoid vaccine. E: The carrier is a protein.

questions.stem: Compared with a plain polysaccharide vaccine, what does the conjugate vaccine add?

options.A: Affinity maturation and memory B cells, but still no response in infants
options.B: Short-lived antibody of the IgM class and no memory
options.C: Cellular immunity through cytotoxic T cells against the capsule
options.D: Protection against the toxin of the carrier and not against the bacterium
options.E: Affinity maturation, memory and improved immune responses in infants

questions.explanation: Conjugate: T-cell help through the carrier protein gives affinity maturation, induction of memory B cells, long-lived antibody production and improved immune responses in infants. A: Responses in infants are improved. B: That describes the plain polysaccharide response. C: Not shown. D: The aim is protection against the polysaccharide-bearing bacterium.

questions.stem: Which statement about toxoid vaccines is correct?

options.A: Bacterial toxins are inactivated with heat; they protect against colonization by the bacterium
options.B: Whole bacteria are inactivated with formalin; boosters are not needed
options.C: Toxins inactivated with formalin; immunity to the toxin's effects, not the infection
options.D: Bacterial toxins are conjugated to polysaccharide; they act as carriers without being immunogenic
options.E: Bacterial toxins are attenuated by culture; reversion to toxicity is frequent

questions.explanation: Toxoid vaccines contain a toxin modified to be non-toxic while keeping immunogenicity, produced by inactivating bacterial toxins with formalin; they make you immune to the harmful effects of the infection rather than to the infection itself. Examples: diphtheria, tetanus (the slide also lists cholera). A: Formalin is used, and immunity is to the toxin's effects. B: Toxoids are modified toxins. D: A toxoid remains immunogenic. E: Not described.

questions.stem: What characterizes viral vector vaccines?

options.A: The target antigen protein is mixed with a virus, inducing humoral responses that need an adjuvant
options.B: A modified virus carries the antigen gene; strong responses without an adjuvant
options.C: The target pathogen is weakened by passage in culture
options.D: mRNA for the antigen is packed in a lipid coat
options.E: The gene for the antigen is inserted in a bacterium licensed for human use

questions.explanation: A modified virus (replicating or not) has its genome altered to express the target pathogen antigen, inducing strong humoral and cellular immune responses without the need for an adjuvant. A: The gene is inserted and no adjuvant is needed. C: That is a live attenuated vaccine. D: That is a nucleic acid vaccine. E: Bacterial vectors are listed as experimental.

questions.stem: What is a potential disadvantage of a human adenovirus vector, and how can it be overcome?

options.A: Pre-existing immunity; use a simian adenovirus
options.B: Reversion to virulence; use an inactivated adenovirus
options.C: Integration into the genome; use an RNA virus
options.D: Poor immunogenicity; add an aluminum adjuvant
options.E: Thermal instability; use a freeze-dried measles vector

questions.explanation: Pre-existing immunity when a vector such as human adenovirus is used; this can be overcome with a simian adenovirus, against which almost no pre-existing immunity exists in humans. B: The problem named is pre-existing immunity. C: Integration risk is listed for DNA vaccines. D: Vector vaccines do not need an adjuvant. E: Not the issue described.

questions.stem: What is the major advantage of nucleic acid vaccines, and which products are given as examples?

options.A: They are stable for years without a cold chain; hepatitis B vaccine
options.B: They need a single dose for lifelong immunity; yellow fever vaccine
options.C: They induce humoral immunity without cellular immunity; Hib vaccine
options.D: Quick to adapt for an emerging pathogen; Pfizer and Moderna vaccines
options.E: They act without being expressed by recipient cells; Ebola vaccine

questions.explanation: DNA or RNA encoding the target antigen is expressed by recipient cells, inducing humoral and cellular responses. A huge advantage is versatility: quick and easy to adapt and produce for an emerging pathogen. Examples: Pfizer and Moderna mRNA vaccines. A: Hepatitis B is a subunit vaccine, and stability is a weakness of mRNA vaccines. B: Yellow fever vaccine is live attenuated. C: They induce both, and Hib is a conjugate vaccine. E: The antigen is expressed by recipient cells, and the Ebola vaccine is viral vectored.

questions.stem: How do DNA and RNA vaccines differ?

options.A: RNA vaccines are stable at room temperature; DNA vaccines do not need to reach the nucleus
options.B: DNA vaccines are expressed in the cytoplasm; RNA vaccines integrate into chromosomes
options.C: DNA vaccines induce humoral responses; RNA vaccines induce cellular responses
options.D: DNA vaccines need a lipid coat; RNA vaccines need a viral vector
options.E: DNA vaccines are stable at room temperature; RNA vaccines do not need to reach the nucleus

questions.explanation: Unlike RNA vaccines, DNA vaccines are stable at room temperature. Unlike DNA vaccines, RNA vaccines do not need to reach the cell nucleus. A: Reversed. B: DNA must reach the nucleus, and integration risk is listed for DNA. C: Both induce both. D: Not the distinction given.

questions.stem: In the table of advantages and disadvantages, which disadvantages are listed for nucleic acid vaccines?

options.A: Weak immunogenicity and requirement for multiple immunizations
options.B: Poor delivery into cells, DNA integration risk, poor mRNA stability
options.C: High storage requirements, poor safety and toxic reversal risk
options.D: Weak and short immunity with requirement for adjuvants
options.E: High purity requirements and possible pre-existing immunity

questions.explanation: Nucleic acid vaccines: high potency, rapid and cost-efficient development; disadvantages are poor intracellular delivery, potential carcinogenesis risk for DNA vaccines due to chromosomal integration, and poor stability of mRNA vaccines. A: Listed for inactivated virus vaccines. C: Listed for attenuated virus vaccines. D: Listed for protein subunit vaccines. E: Listed for viral vector vaccines.

questions.stem: A child with a combined immunodeficiency needs immunization advice. Which statement matches the lecture?

options.A: Non-live vaccines are safe but may not protect in combined immunodeficiency
options.B: Non-live vaccines may replicate uncontrollably and must be avoided
options.C: Live vaccines pose no risk and are preferred because immunity is stronger
options.D: Non-live vaccines pose no risk and protect fully without B cells
options.E: Live and non-live vaccines carry the same risk of uncontrolled replication

questions.explanation: Live vaccines may replicate in an uncontrolled manner in immunocompromised individuals. Non-live vaccines pose no risk to them, although they may not confer protection in those with B-cell or combined immunodeficiency. B: That risk belongs to live vaccines. C: Live vaccines may replicate in an uncontrolled manner. D: They may not confer protection in these patients. E: Non-live vaccines do not replicate.

questions.stem: How do adjuvants enhance the immunogenicity of a vaccine?

options.A: They can act like antibodies, neutralizing the vaccine antigen slowly
options.B: They can act like MHC molecules, presenting peptide directly to T cells
options.C: They can act like PAMPs, activating innate immunity and APCs
options.D: They replicate in the host and prolong antigen exposure
options.E: They link polysaccharide to a carrier protein

questions.explanation: Adjuvants are substances added to vaccines to enhance immunogenicity; they can act like PAMPs, triggering the innate response so that vaccine components are seen as a threat, with activation and maturation of APCs. A: Not the mechanism. B: Not the mechanism. D: Adjuvants are not living. E: That defines a conjugate vaccine.

questions.stem: Adjuvants fall into two classes. Which pairing of class and role is correct?

options.A: Delivery systems activate the innate immune system directly; immune potentiators concentrate and display antigens
options.B: Delivery systems are cytokines; immune potentiators are cationic microparticles
options.C: Delivery systems preserve the vaccine; immune potentiators stabilize it
options.D: Delivery systems concentrate and display antigens; immune potentiators activate the innate immune system directly
options.E: Delivery systems carry the antigen gene; immune potentiators are viral vectors

questions.explanation: Delivery systems (such as cationic microparticles) concentrate and display antigens in repetitious patterns and help localize them. Immune potentiators (such as cytokines or PRR ligands) activate the innate immune system directly. A: Reversed. B: The examples are swapped. C: Those are roles of preservatives and stabilizers. E: Not adjuvant classes.

questions.stem: Which adjuvants are used routinely in licensed vaccines, and which other vaccine components are mentioned with an allergy warning?

options.A: Polysorbate 80 as adjuvant; aluminum salts as stabilizers
options.B: Gelatine as adjuvant; liposomes as preservatives
options.C: Tetanus toxoid as adjuvant; formalin as emulsifier
options.D: Cytokines as routine adjuvants; aluminum hydroxide as preservative
options.E: Aluminum salts; emulsifiers such as polysorbate 80, and stabilizers

questions.explanation: Aluminum salts (aluminum hydroxide, aluminum phosphate, alum) are routine adjuvants; liposome-based adjuvants and oil-in-water emulsions were licensed more recently. Vaccines also contain preservatives, emulsifiers (polysorbate 80) and stabilizers (gelatine, sorbitol): be aware of allergies. A: Aluminum salts are the adjuvants. B: Gelatine is a stabilizer. C: Tetanus toxoid is a carrier protein in conjugate vaccines. D: Aluminum salts are the routine adjuvants.

questions.stem: Which pairing of infection and cancer is used to illustrate vaccination against cancer-inducing agents?

options.A: HPV16 and HPV18: liver cancer; hepatitis B virus: cervical cancer
options.B: Helicobacter pylori: cervical cancer; HPV16: stomach cancer
options.C: HPV16 and HPV18: cervical cancer; hepatitis B virus: liver cancer
options.D: Hepatitis A virus: liver cancer; HPV6: cervical cancer
options.E: Epstein–Barr virus: stomach cancer; hepatitis B virus: cervical cancer

questions.explanation: Strategies include vaccines targeting agents that induce cancer: HPV16 and HPV18 (cervical cancer), Helicobacter pylori (stomach cancer; listed on the slide although it is a bacterium), hepatitis B virus (liver cancer). A: Reversed. B: H. pylori is linked to stomach cancer and HPV to cervical cancer. D: The slide names hepatitis B and HPV16/18. E: Not the pairs listed.

questions.stem: What is the second strategy of vaccination against cancer?

options.A: Making "cold" tumors "hot" and amenable to checkpoint blockade
options.B: Inducing tolerance in "hot" tumors to convert them into "cold" tumors resistant to checkpoint blockade
options.C: Transferring preformed antibodies against tumor antigens
options.D: Attenuating tumor cells by culture and injecting them live
options.E: Blocking herd transmission of tumor cells

questions.explanation: Vaccines can induce immune responses in "cold" tumors that do not appear immunogenic on their own, potentially converting them to "hot" tumors amenable to checkpoint blockade therapy. B: Reversed. C: That would be passive immunization. D: Not described. E: Not applicable.
